div.p: Introduction: Pediatric optic nerve sheath meningiomas (ONSMs) are rare and have an aggressive presentation often resulting in rapid vision decline. Here, we report a case of a right cavernous sinus meningioma (CSM) with a delayed diagnosis of concomitant bilateral ONSMs, ultimately leading to permanent bilateral blindness. Case Presentation: A 7-year-old boy with a history of a right trochlear nerve palsy and amblyopia presented with worsening right eye vision. An MRI revealed a right CSM that was resected; however, the patient experienced a progressive visual acuity decline from 20/60 right eye and 20/40 left eye to light perception right eye and 20/400 left eye, along with bilateral optic atrophy appreciated on optical coherence tomography. Repeat evaluation of the brain MRIs revealed bilateral ONSMs characterized by a tram-track appearance. The visual acuity remained unimproved 3 years after optic canal decompression with optic nerve sheath fenestration followed by proton beam radiation. Conclusion: Pediatric ONSM is rare, with a high risk of permanent blindness in children. Intracranial meningioma and unexplained painless vision loss should prompt a careful evaluation of orbital neuroimaging for this condition.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Classically, optic nerve sheath meningiomas (ONSMs) are present with a triad of progressive vision loss, optic atrophy, and retinal choroidal shunt vessels on fundoscopy [1]. ONSMs account for 1-2% of all meningiomas and 2% of all orbital tumors in adults, with unknown pediatric prevalence, although certainly more rare [1]. Notably, pediatric patients with ONSM often experience a more aggressive disease course with a rapid visual decline and a higher risk of intracranial extension with recurrence [2]. Here, we report a right cavernous sinus meningioma (CSM) in a pediatric patient with delayed diagnosis of concomitant bilateral ONSMs causing permanent bilateral vision loss. To our knowledge, this is the first case of pediatric CSM with ONSM documented in the literature.

div.head: Case Report
div.p: A 7-year-old boy with a 3-year history of right trochlear nerve palsy and a 1-year history of amblyopia in the right eye presented to a tertiary children's hospital with worsening right eye vision. The patient had no history of radiation exposure. Family

div.head: Discussion
div.p: After conducting a literature review on 23 June 2025, utilizing PubMed and Google Scholar using the keywords pediatric, cavernous sinus meningioma, and optic nerve sheath meningioma, we did not find any prior reports of pediatric CSM and concomitant ONSM. This

div.head: Case Reports in Ophthalmology
div.p: condition led to bilateral blindness that persisted despite optic canal decompression, optic nerve sheath fenestration, and proton beam radiation.

ONSM is present in 6.8% of neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) patients [3]. Other hereditary cancer predisposition syndromes, including Cowden syndrome (PTEN), Gorlin syndrome (PTCH1), and Werner syndrome (WRN), have also been associated with the development of multiple meningiomas [4]. Genetic testing in this patient for NF2, PTEN, and PTCH1 was negative (WRN was not assessed). However, the sensitivity of these genetic panels is variable, and mosaic variants may not be detected reliably. Notably, drusenoid deposits were identified in the macula of the left eye, an unexplained finding not previously reported in association with ONSM or CSM, although they have been associated with other genetic conditions [5]. Due to poor fixation, identification of drusenoid deposits in the right macula was not possible.
Usually, for ONSMs observation is appropriate if the visual acuity remains stable [6].

Most often, treatment is indicated for risk of intracranial expansion. Radiotherapy options include proton beam radiation and stereotactic radiotherapy. Proton beam radiation and stereotactic radiotherapy decrease collateral radiation, particularly advantageous in children due to long-term risk of secondary malignancy. Mifepristone may be considered in rare, refractory cases, but is not standard of care and was not attempted for our patient [7].

Although controversial, optic canal decompression and optic nerve sheath fenestration have been advocated by some to relieve local pressure and obtain a biopsy [8,9]. In this case, these surgeries were performed prophylactically to prevent further vision loss from nerve

div.head: Case Reports in Ophthalmology
div.p: compression that may result from local swelling during radiation. Following surgery vision remained stable but without improvement.

While progressive vision loss for this patient occurred at other times, precipitous vision loss occurred following uncomplicated strabismus surgery in the operative eye. To our knowledge, there are no previous cases reporting visual acuity decline immediately after strabismus surgery in the setting of optic nerve tumors, although meningiomaassociated edema has been reported following radiosurgery [10]. Potential etiologies include local inflammatory changes contributing to tumor edema or unrelated tumor growth.

The patient's early presentation with right-sided vision loss and impaired color vision in the left eye, in the absence of retinal pathology, suggested bilateral optic neuropathy before radiographic findings were discovered. Biopsy of the optic nerve canalicular dura obtained during CSM resection was negative. However, other skull base specimens, including from the right petroclival ligament, were positive for meningioma. Incomplete sampling of the optic nerve sheath may have missed focal meningioma infiltration. Without evidence for direct extension, there may have been multiple primary meningioma sites in this case. Together, these factors contributed to the ONSMs being missed for over 4 years.

A delay in radiographic diagnosis of ONSM is a common occurrence; the majority of cases in prior reports were missed or delayed (71% at one institution), often resulting in vision loss [10]. ONSMs were often missed when lacking a neuroradiology consultation, fine cuts through the orbit, or contrast [11,12]. Some of these factors may have Case Reports in Ophthalmology influenced this case. Early neuroradiology involvement, contrast-enhanced orbital MRI, and repeat imaging in the setting of persistent visual acuity decline may help reduce such diagnostic delays.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Pediatric ONSM should be considered in the differential diagnosis of intracranial meningioma and unexplained painless vision loss, prompting careful evaluation of orbital neuroimaging.

div.head: Statement of Ethics
div.p: Ethical approval is not required for this study in accordance with local or national guidelines. Written informed consent was obtained from the parent of the patient, who provided consent on the patient's behalf for publication of the case details and any accompanying images.

figure.figDesc: history was negative for malignancy or neurofibromatosis, except for a maternal grandfather with glioblastoma multiforme. The patient had a small intermittent right hypertropia, consistent with a right superior oblique palsy. Nystagmus was not present in either eye. Brain MRI revealed a right CSM. UW-OncoPlex ™ testing (NF1, NF2, SMARCB1) and Invitae pediatric nervous system/brain tumor panel with add-on analysis of basal cell nevus syndrome panel (that includes PTEN and PTCH1) were negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed mildly elevated neutrophils and normal glucose without malignant cells. Although the visual acuity remained stable in the left eye at 20/40, progressive right eye visual decline from 20/70 to 20/200 prompted a meningioma resection and a partial right optic canal decompression (shown in Fig. 1). Five biopsy samples were taken from multiple locations (including the right petroclival ligament, the intradural clinoid area, and the optic canal), of which four showed WHO Grade 1 meningioma with no tumor in the optic canal dura. Postoperatively, the patient received oral dexamethasone 2 mg every 6 h for 3 days. Two weeks postoperatively, the visual acuity improved to 20/60 in the right eye, with no change in the left eye. Two months postoperatively, the right eye visual acuity declined to 20/800. The superior oblique palsy was no longer detectable due to inability to conduct cover testing in the setting of poor visual acuity. The pupils were reactive to light without a relative afferent pupillary defect. Ishihara color plates were 0/11 left eye (unable right eye). External and slit lamp examinations were unremarkable. Dilated fundus examination showed mild pallor and peripapillary atrophy without disk edema (cupto-disk ratio 0.3) bilaterally. Cycloplegic refraction revealed +1.00 +1.00 axis 80 and +2.00 sphere, respectively. Repeat MRIs were interpreted as showing no tumor recurrence. Peripapillary optical coherence tomography (OCT) using the Spectralis (Heidelberg Engineering, Germany) revealed bilateral diffuse retinal nerve fiber layer thinning (global thickness 50 μm right eye and 49 μm left eye), shown in Figure 2. Due to unexplained left eye optic atrophy in the setting of only right-sided CSM, OPA-1 genetic testing for autosomal dominant optic atrophy was obtained and was negative. At 18 months postoperatively, the patient developed a sensory intermittent exotropia of 25 prism diopters at distance, orthotropia at near, with full motility. Additionally, OCT revealed new subtle parafoveal drusenoid deposits in the retinal pigment Case Reports in Ophthalmology epithelium of the left eye, shown in Figure 2. A repeat brain MRI was interpreted as showing no tumor recurrence and normal orbits. Following uncomplicated strabismus surgery (right medial rectus resection and lateral rectus recession), the visual acuity declined to light perception in the right eye and 20/60 in the left eye. With some fluctuations, vision loss persisted 4 months later in spite of a stable cycloplegic refraction, OCT, and brain MRI. Another 7 months later, the patient noted left eye vision loss. Repeat brain MRI and OCT revealed no change. The visual acuity was light perception in the right eye and 20/400 in the left eye. Left macular drusenoid deposits appeared progressively enlarged but with no vision-threatening changes, shown in

figure.head: Figure 2 .
figure.figDesc: Figure 2. Due to unexplained left eye vision loss, previous MRIs were carefully reviewed again with the neuroradiologist, who noted the presence of bilateral intraconal and intracanalicular perineural enhancements with tram-track appearance consistent with ONSMs, shown in Figure 3. Upon careful review, these findings were present in all scans over the prior 4 years. No other known family members exhibited ONSM, CSM, optic atrophy, or macular disease. To decrease local effects of radiation, the patient underwent bilateral optic canal decompression and optic nerve sheath fenestration followed by proton beam radiation (50.4 Cobalt-Gray equivalents in 28 fractions over 37 days to the bilateral optic nerves and optic chiasm). Three years later, the visual acuity remained at light perception in the right eye and 20/400 in the left eye with mild, non-visually significant postradiation posterior subcapsular cataracts and stable optic atrophy. The CARE Checklist has been completed by the authors for this case report, attached as online supplementary material (for all online suppl. material, see https://doi.org/10.1159/ 000549940).

figure.head: Fig. 1 .
figure.figDesc: Fig. 1. Brain MRI's (T1-weighted post-contrast) demonstrating right-sided CSM before (black arrow demonstrates tumor) (a) and after meningioma resection and partial right optic canal decompression (b). Postsurgically, MRI demonstrated right-sided postoperative changes without left-sided involvement. The imaging plane was optimized for visualization of the cavernous sinus rather than the optic nerves. See Figure 3 for optic nerve imaging.

figure.head: Fig. 2 .
figure.figDesc: Fig. 2. OCT findings demonstrating bilateral optic nerve and macular abnormalities. Peripapillary RNFL OCT obtained 2 months after initial CSM resection showed diffuse RNFL thinning bilaterally. Global thickness was 50 µm right eye with a visual acuity of 20/800 (a) and 49 µm left eye with a visual acuity of 20/40 (b). Horizontal macular OCT of the left eye revealed progressively enlarging perifoveal drusenoid deposits (arrows) at 18 months (c) and almost 3 years postoperatively (d). Due to poor fixation, macular OCT scans were difficult to obtain for the right eye. NF2 gene testing was negative. RNFL, retinal nerve fiber layer.

figure.head: Fig. 3 .
figure.figDesc: Fig. 3. T1 brain MRI sequences demonstrating ONSMs (arrows), missed at the time of imaging. a, c, e Axial images demonstrated a classic tram-track appearance. b, d, f Corresponding coronal images revealed a doughnut sign surrounding the optic nerves, especially obvious in (b). a, b At the time of CSM resection, preoperative visual acuity was 20/200 right eye and 20/40 left eye. c, d At 1 year postoperatively, visual acuity was 20/400 right eye and 20/30 left eye. e, f At 3 years postoperatively, visual acuity was light perception right eye and 20/400 left eye.
